summary: Describes an option for negotiating header compression on IP datagrams sent over the Point-to-Point Protocol. It extends the PPP control protocols for both IPv4 and IPv6. It was replaced by RFC 3544.

eli5.summary: Two computers connected by a phone-line style link can agree to use shorter labels on their messages. This document explains how they agree on that.

questions: what are the ppp protocol identifiers for compressed packets
why share context identifier space between ipv4 and ipv6
subtitle: Letting computers on a point-to-point link agree to shrink IP headers to save bandwidth.

tldr.problem: IP headers take up space on slow links like dial-up modems. Two computers at each end of a PPP link may want to use header compression but need to negotiate the parameters first.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2509 defines how two PPP endpoints negotiate IP Header Compression using the network control protocols for IPv4 and IPv6, specifying a configuration option that lists the compression parameters both sides will use.
tldr.outcome: The RFC enabled header compression on PPP links for both TCP (with delta encoding) and UDP/RTP traffic. It was later superseded by RFC 3544, which extended the framework.

today: RFC 2509 is obsoleted by RFC 3544, which extended the framework with additional capabilities. Header compression over PPP is now less common because broadband connections have made the bandwidth savings less critical, but the technique remains relevant for low-bandwidth and long-delay networks.

sections.title: Why Compress IP Headers
sections.content:
IP Header Compression (IPHC) is a technique that removes redundancy from the headers of IP packets, especially TCP and UDP headers, to save space on low-bandwidth links. A typical IP and TCP header together are 40 bytes; with compression, that can shrink to a few bytes for packets in an existing conversation.

The Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) is used for direct links such as dial-up modems and serial connections. RFC 2509 specifies how two PPP endpoints can negotiate compression parameters so they both use the same algorithm and the same settings. Without this negotiation, one side might try to compress while the other expects uncompressed packets, causing the connection to fail.
sections.eli5: Imagine sending many postcards on a slow mail service. Instead of writing 'Dear Friend, I'm fine, From Me' on each one, you could agree beforehand on a shorthand like 'DF01' that you both understand. That's what header compression does.

sections.title: The Compression Framework
sections.content:
IPHC supports compression of both IPv4 and IPv6 headers in combination with TCP, UDP, and RTP. The technique relies on the fact that in an ongoing stream of packets, most header fields stay the same (same source and destination, same port numbers). IPHC sends the full header once, then subsequent packets in that flow send only the fields that change, encoded as small differences (deltas).

PPP negotiates link parameters using network control protocols (NCPs): IPCP for IPv4 and IPV6CP for IPv6. RFC 2509 adds a new compression protocol value and configuration option to these NCPs. The negotiation happens before any data transfer, allowing both sides to agree on the compression parameters.

Separate context identifier spaces are maintained for TCP traffic and for non-TCP traffic (UDP and RTP). This separation ensures that switching between traffic types does not cause errors in decompression.
sections.eli5: Two computers speak to each other before they start sending data, saying 'let's use compression' and 'here's how we'll identify which packets belong to which conversation'. Then they can send short headers until the connection ends.

sections.title: Negotiation Parameters
sections.content:
The PPP configuration option for IPHC contains several fields that both sides agree on:

TCP_SPACE is the number of compression contexts (conversation slots) for TCP traffic, ranging from 0 to 255. A higher value lets the compressor track more simultaneous TCP flows but uses more memory.

NON_TCP_SPACE covers contexts for UDP and RTP traffic, with a suggested value of 15. The suggested value for TCP_SPACE is also 15.

F_MAX_PERIOD and F_MAX_TIME limit how many compressed headers the compressor can send between full (uncompressed) headers. F_MAX_PERIOD is a packet count (suggested 256), and F_MAX_TIME is a time interval in seconds (suggested 5 seconds). Periodic full headers ensure that if a compressed header is lost, the decompressor can resynchronize.

MAX_HEADER specifies the largest header size (in octets) that will be compressed. A suggested value is 168 octets, large enough for common combinations of IP, TCP, and options.
sections.eli5: The two sides agree on how many ongoing conversations they'll track, how often to send a full header instead of a short one, and how big a header can be before it's too big to bother compressing.

sections.title: Packet Types on the Wire
sections.content:
Once both sides agree to use IPHC, they need distinct PPP protocol field values to identify what type of compressed packet they are sending. RFC 2509 defines nine new values:

FULL_HEADER (0x0061) contains an uncompressed IP header. This is sent periodically so the decompressor can resynchronize.

COMPRESSED_TCP (0x0063) is an IP packet with a compressed TCP header using delta encoding.

COMPRESSED_TCP_NODELTA (0x2063) is a variant that omits delta encoding, used when delta encoding is not appropriate.

COMPRESSED_NON_TCP (0x0065) covers compressed UDP or RTP headers (with either 8-bit or 16-bit context identifiers; the decompressor determines which from the packet's contents).

For RTP compression, additional protocol identifiers include COMPRESSED_RTP_8 (0x0069) and COMPRESSED_RTP_16 (0x2069), plus COMPRESSED_UDP_8 (0x0067) and COMPRESSED_UDP_16 (0x2067). A CONTEXT_STATE message (0x2065) lets the decompressor tell the compressor about errors.
sections.eli5: Each type of compressed packet gets a number so the receiver knows what it's looking at: 'this is a full header, resync yourself' or 'this is a short TCP packet, look up context 5 and fill in the blanks'.

sections.title: Sharing Context Across IPv4 and IPv6
sections.content:
Both IPv4 and IPv6 can use IPHC, and both can be negotiated over the same PPP link using separate NCPs. However, the context identifier space is shared between IPv4 and IPv6 compressed packets. This complicates the decompressor: it must track which parameters apply to IPv4 contexts and which to IPv6, since the two may have different TCP_SPACE and NON_TCP_SPACE values.

When allocating context identifiers, the compression engine assigns them from a shared pool. When decompressing, the decompressor examines the context state (including the IP version in the packet) to apply the correct decompression parameters. This sharing is possible because TCP and non-TCP contexts are already separated, so the decompressor can navigate the complexity.
sections.eli5: If both IPv4 and IPv6 packets are using the same link, they share the same context numbers, but the decompressor has to know which rules apply to each IP version.
